FCExercise

FractionsArithmeticAlgebra
Game: Two fractions are shown with a third one between them that is not really between them yet; make it fit, then check.
How to play: Press the digits of the middle fraction to raise them, or select one and type a digit, until the middle fraction is bigger than one of the other two and smaller than the other. Then press Check.

Look for the math

The standard way to compare a/c and b/d is cross-multiplication: a/c > b/d exactly when ad > bc. But the products are often not needed.

Shortcuts

With the same denominator, the bigger numerator wins: a/c > b/c when a > b. With the same numerator, the smaller denominator wins: a/c > a/d when c < d. A proper fraction grows when you add 1 to both its parts: a/c < (a+1)/(c+1) when a < c. The test checked all three for every value up to 40 or 60.

The trick: a fraction in between

To compare 7/12 and 4/9, notice that 7/12 > 6/12 = 1/2 while 4/9 = 8/18 < 9/18 = 1/2. So 7/12 > 1/2 > 4/9, and no multiplication was needed. The exercise asks you for that middle fraction. The applet starts you with a guess that is always just outside the pair (the test confirmed that for 200,000 generated pairs), and Check accepts any fraction between the two, the ends included. The test compared that rule with exact cross-multiplication for more than a million combinations.

Common denominators and simplest form

“Use common denominator” rewrites both fractions over the least common denominator, where the bigger numerator wins. “Simplify” reduces fractions to lowest terms, which often makes the middle one easier to see. Neither changes a value; the test checked it.

The applet lets you check a middle fraction with a denominator of 0; this page asks for a real one.

Try 5/9 and 4/7. Is 1/2 between them? What about 4/8? Use the common denominator button to see what is going on.
